passages.happening:
The writer now explains what a high priest is, so that his readers can see why Jesus is one.

“Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (verse 1).

“He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is beset by weakness. That is why he is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people” (verses 2-3).

“No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The writer names three things true of every high priest in Israel.

First, he is one of the people. He is ‘appointed from among men’, so that he can stand for them before God, bringing their gifts and their sacrifices.

Second, he is gentle, because he is weak too. He knows what it is to fail, so he can ‘deal gently’ with people who sin because they do not know better or have lost their way. On the Day of Atonement, the high priest first offered a sacrifice for his own sins, and only then for the people's.

Third, he does not appoint himself. The honour is given by God. Aaron, Moses' brother, did not make himself high priest. God called him.

Notice how respectfully the writer speaks of Israel's priesthood. He describes it as God's own arrangement, a good gift, with a gentle, humble priest at its heart. Then, in the next verses, he will show how Jesus fits each point, in reverse order.
passages.ot:
God called Aaron and his sons to be priests: “Next, have your brother Aaron brought to you from among the Israelites, along with his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, to serve Me as priests” (Exodus 28:1).

The high priest offered first for himself, then for the people. On the Day of Atonement, “Aaron is to present the bull for his sin offering and make atonement for himself and his household” (Leviticus 16:6). At the first sacrifices, Moses told him, “sacrifice your sin offering and your burnt offering to make atonement for yourself and for the people” (Leviticus 9:7).

The danger of taking the honour for oneself is told in the story of Korah, who rebelled against Aaron's priesthood (Numbers 16). Afterwards the bronze from the rebels' censers was made into a covering for the altar, “a reminder to the Israelites that no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the LORD” (Numbers 16:40).
passages.asks: A good priest is gentle with the weak because he knows his own weakness. Ask whether you are gentle with people who fail, or harsh. Ask what it would mean to remember your own weakness the next time someone else's is in front of you. And ask whether you are taking on honours or roles that are not yours to take.

passages.t: Called by God: Son and priest forever
passages.happening:
Now the writer shows how Jesus fits. He begins with the last point, being called.

“So also Christ did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest, but He was called by the One who said to Him: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.’ And in another passage God says: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
Jesus did not make himself high priest. God called him, as he called Aaron.

The writer gives two passages of Scripture as God's call. The first, ‘You are My Son’, he has already used in 1:5. It shows that the one God calls is his Son. The second is new: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’ It shows that the Son is also a priest.

This would have surprised the first readers. In Israel, kings and priests came from different tribes. Kings came from Judah, priests from Levi. Jesus was from Judah. So how can he be a priest? The answer is in that strange name, Melchizedek. The writer will explain it in chapter 7. For now he simply plants the name, and it will come back again and again.

‘The order of Melchizedek’ means ‘after the pattern of Melchizedek’. ‘Forever’ means this priesthood will not end, as every human priest's service ended with his death.
passages.ot:
Verse 5 quotes Psalm 2:7 again, God's word to his king: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (Psalm 2:7).

Verse 6 quotes Psalm 110, the psalm that begins with God seating a king at his right hand: “The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’” (Psalm 110:4). In its own setting, as the site's note on Psalm 110 explains, it is a word to a king of David's line in Jerusalem, giving him a priestly role after the pattern of Melchizedek, the king and priest of Salem in Abraham's day (Genesis 14:18-20). In Israel kings and priests were kept apart; this psalm reaches back before Levi was born to find a king who was also a priest.

Melchizedek is named in no other book of the New Testament. Hebrews alone quotes Psalm 110:4. It joins it to Psalm 110:1, which it has already quoted (1:13): the same king who sits at God's right hand is a priest forever.
passages.hard:
Who was Melchizedek, and why does Hebrews make so much of him?

Melchizedek appears in only two places in the Old Testament: three verses in Genesis 14 and one in Psalm 110. Genesis tells of a king of Salem, ‘priest of God Most High’, who blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him. Salem is usually identified with Jerusalem. Most readers, Jewish and Christian, take him as a real king who worshipped the true God. The psalm then makes him the pattern for a king who is also a priest.

Hebrews uses him because he shows that there was a priesthood older than Aaron's and not based on family line. That is how Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, can be a priest. Chapter 7 sets out the whole argument, and the notes there, like the notes on Genesis 14 and Psalm 110, take care not to say more about Melchizedek than the Bible does.
passages.asks: Jesus did not take glory for himself; he was called. Ask where you are tempted to make your own name, and where you need to wait for God's call. And ask what it means to have a priest whose service will never end, who will still be praying for you when every human helper is gone.

passages.t: Loud cries and tears: he learned obedience
passages.happening:
Now the writer shows that Jesus, like every high priest, knew weakness from the inside.

“During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence” (verse 7).

“Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered. And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him and was designated by God as high priest in the order of Melchizedek” (verses 8-10).
passages.hearers:
These are some of the most tender verses in the Bible about Jesus. The Son of God prayed with ‘loud cries and tears’. He was not acting. He was in anguish. Most readers think of the night in the garden of Gethsemane before his arrest, when he prayed for the cup of suffering to pass from him, and yet said to his Father, ‘not what I will’. Others think the words gather up the whole of his suffering, including his cry from the cross.

‘Offered up’ is the word Hebrews uses for a priest offering a sacrifice. So his prayers are pictured as a priest's offering.

‘Reverence’ means a deep, trusting awe of God, the attitude of one who bows to God's will.

‘He learned obedience from what He suffered.’ In Greek the two verbs, ‘learned’ and ‘suffered’, sound almost the same, and Greek writers had long used the pair to say that people learn by suffering. The writer uses the familiar saying for something new.

Then, made perfect, he became ‘the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him’. He obeyed the Father; those who belong to him obey him.
passages.ot:
The psalms are full of prayers with cries and tears, and of God hearing them. “For He has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted. He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help” (Psalm 22:24). That is the turn in the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross. And, “I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice— my appeal for mercy” (Psalm 116:1).

Isaiah's servant of the LORD speaks of an obedience that went through suffering: “The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back. I offered My back to those who struck Me” (Isaiah 50:5-6).

‘Eternal salvation’ echoes Isaiah's promise to Israel: “But Israel will be saved by the LORD with an everlasting salvation” (Isaiah 45:17).
passages.hard:
‘He learned obedience.’ ‘Having been made perfect.’ Does this mean Jesus was once disobedient, or once less than he should be?

No, and the letter itself rules it out. He was tempted ‘yet was without sin’ (4:15). He was ‘holy, innocent, undefiled’ (7:26). Learning obedience does not mean moving from disobedience to obedience. It means coming to know obedience from the inside, by actually obeying when it cost him everything: in the garden, under arrest, on the cross. A son who has always loved his father still learns what that love costs on the day he is asked to give his life.

‘Made perfect’ in Hebrews means complete, fully qualified for his work. In the Greek Old Testament the same word was used for setting a priest apart for his office. By his suffering, death and rising, Jesus was made complete as the Saviour and high priest of his people. He did not become more God or more good.

The church confesses this together. Jesus Christ is ‘very God of very God’, in the words of the Nicene Creed, and he ‘was made man’. The Council of Chalcedon in AD 451 confessed him as ‘truly God and truly man’, ‘in all things like unto us, without sin’. His tears and his learning belong to his true humanity, and they take nothing from his being God.

And what of verse 7: if he was heard, why did he die? Readers answer in more than one way. Some say his deepest prayer was for the Father's will to be done (Mark 14:36), and that prayer was granted. Many say he was saved out of death rather than from dying: God answered by raising him. Others say God heard him by holding him through it all. On every reading, God's answer was not escape from suffering but victory through it.

If you are praying with tears and wondering whether you are heard, this verse is for you. The Son of God prayed that way too. The psalms are full of such prayers, and God kept them in his book. If your nights are full of tears now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears. Ask whether you allow yourself to pray like that, or whether you think God wants only calm, tidy prayers. Ask what obedience is costing you, and whether you can trust that it costs nothing he did not pay first. And ask whether you are following the one who is the source of eternal salvation.

passages.happening:
Now the writer stops, almost in frustration. He wants to explain Melchizedek, but his readers are not ready.

“We have much to say about this, but it is hard to explain, because you are dull of hearing” (verse 11).

“Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to reteach you the basic principles of God’s word. You need milk, not solid food! For everyone who lives on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness. But solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil” (verses 12-14).
passages.hearers:
This is the start of the third warning passage, which runs to 6:12.

‘Dull of hearing’ means slow and sluggish in listening. The Greek says ‘you have become’ dull. They were not always this way. They had drifted into it.

They had been believers long enough to teach others. Instead they needed someone to go over the ABCs again. ‘Basic principles’ uses a word for the letters of the alphabet.

Milk and solid food was a common picture for beginners and grown-ups in learning. Greek teachers used it, and Paul used it with the Corinthians. ‘Mature’ belongs to the same family of words as ‘made perfect’ in verse 9.

Notice what maturity is. It is not knowing more facts. It is having ‘trained their senses to distinguish good from evil’. The word ‘trained’ is the word for exercise in a gymnasium. Maturity comes from practice, from using what you know, again and again, until you can tell right from wrong in real life.
passages.ot:
‘God’s word’ in verse 12 uses a Greek phrase Paul uses in Romans for Israel's Scriptures: the Jewish people “have been entrusted with the very words of God” (Romans 3:2). The readers knew the Scriptures; the trouble was that they were not growing in them.

The Old Testament prizes the same practical wisdom, the ability to tell good from evil. Solomon asked for it: “Therefore give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9).

And the psalms invite every believer to taste God's goodness for themselves: “Taste and see that the LORD is good” (Psalm 34:8).
passages.hard:
Is this a rebuke of people who find the Bible hard to read, or who learn slowly?

No. The writer is not rebuking people for being young in faith, or for finding study hard, or for having little schooling. He is rebuking people who had been taught for years and had stopped listening and stopped growing. The problem was a sluggish heart, not a slow mind.

And growth here is measured by practice, not by knowledge alone. A person who knows little but obeys what they know is growing. A person who knows much and uses none of it is still on milk.
passages.asks: Maturity comes by practice. Ask how long you have followed Jesus, and whether you are growing or standing still. Ask where you have heard the same truth many times without acting on it. And ask what one thing you already know that you could begin to practise this week.
